frames.narration: Half of all customers are on the orders service. Customer 4211 changes the delivery address of order o-77 in the app. The request reaches the router, which has one rule for orders: a hash of the customer id, and a share set to 50%.
The hash of 4211 falls in the migrated half, and it always will, so this customer never flips between the two sides. The router sends the request to the orders service.

The service updates the order and, in the same local transaction, writes an event to its outbox table with the row's new version, 7. Either both are saved or neither. No call goes to the monolith's database at all.

Meanwhile the router has also sent a copy of the customer's last read to the parity checker as shadow traffic. It asks both sides for the same order and compares the two answers, ignoring the shadow answer for the customer.

The relay reads the outbox and applies the event to the monolith's database, retrying until it works. It only writes a row if the event's version is newer than the one there, so a repeated or late event changes nothing.

A legacy report still reads the old order tables. A few seconds later it sees the new address, because the relay copied it. If it had run during the delay, it would have shown the old address once, which that report accepts.

At night the parity checker compares both databases row by row. It finds 38 of 100,000 orders that differ, 0.04%, all within the relay's delay window or caused by a known rounding rule, and logs each one. The mismatch rate is under the 0.1% target, so the share may be raised.

Months later the share has been 100% for a whole month-end close. The legacy reports now call the orders API, the relay back to the old database is switched off, and the monolith's orders module and tables are removed. The route is plain, with no flag.
